name: eval_content_drift
prompt: I've been tracking my skill across v3, v4, v5 and the pass rate is creeping up. But I realize I reworded some eval prompts and swapped a couple of gold answers along the way, though the item_id column names stayed the same. How do I know whether the improvement is real or just my eval changing under me?
response:
This is exactly the problem `reference/13_item_drift.md` was built for. The short answer: **column names are not trustworthy keys for a measurement model — content hashes are.** A reworded prompt under the same `item_id` is a different item, and a swapped gold answer can flip difficulty direction entirely. Your v3→v5 gain is a mix of real skill improvement and ruler change, and right now you can't tell them apart.

## What you need to do

**Step 1 — Detect which items actually changed.**

If you logged the item text (or the eval prompt + gold answer) alongside each run's scores, run:

```bash
python scripts/item_drift.py manifest.csv \
  --text-col item_text --run-col run_id --score-col score \
  --out drift.json
```

It hashes content per `item_id` per run and flags every case where the hash changed. It also reports the **stable anchor set** (items that were identical across all three runs) and the pass-rate swing on each drifted item. A big swing on a "cosmetic" reword is the tell that the edit changed what the item actually measures.

If you *didn't* log item text per run, check git history — the eval file at each version commit is the source of truth. Reconstruct the manifest from those snapshots.

**Step 2 — Separate the comparison.**

Once you have the stable anchors vs. drifted items:

- **Stable anchors only** → the only valid evidence about v3→v5 skill improvement. Compute pass-rate change on this subset. If it's still creeping up, the improvement is real (at least on the parts of the eval that didn't change).
- **Drifted items** → treat as new items from the rewrite date forward. Pass-rate change on these conflates "better skill" with "different task" — don't use them for the longitudinal comparison.
- If the stable anchor set is tiny (say, 3 items out of 20), you can't support a strong claim either way — your ruler changed too much.

**Step 3 — Fix the design going forward.**

Suffix each item with its content hash so rewrites become explicit new items (`q07@a1b2` vs `q07@9f3c`). Deliberately freeze a subset of cases as your **anchor set** — these never get reworded, so every future version can be placed on the same scale. For v6 onward, calibrate anchors once, then score new versions against the fixed anchors via `scripts/irt_latent.py --fixed-items`.

## The uncomfortable honest read on your current data

Without logged content, the best you can do retroactively is reconstruct from git. If git shows the rewords happened between v3→v4, then:
- v3 vs. v4: potentially confounded on those items
- v4 vs. v5: cleaner if you didn't reword again

Even if the stable-anchor subset is small, it's more trustworthy evidence than the full suite. Report the gain on that subset explicitly, note how many items were stable, and call the drifted-item gains provisional until you have a fixed anchor design in place.

assertions.text: Frames it as measurement invariance / drift and says column names can't be trusted as item keys
Recommends content hashing to detect drift and treating changed items as new (not pooling across the change)
Recommends anchor/common-item linking to put runs on a comparable scale
Warns the observed improvement may be instrument drift, not a real gain
